record.paper_title: Optimal Algorithms for Numerical Integration: Recent Results and Open Problems
record.original_question: For one-dimensional numerical integration, two universal randomized strategies are highlighted: a randomly shifted midpoint rule with a random number n in {m,m+1,...,2m} for periodic functions, and, for non-periodic functions, a method that first interpolates f at Chebyshev points by a polynomial f_m and then applies separation of the main part together with Monte Carlo to f-f_m. How do these two approaches compare in detail, both theoretically and practically, in dimension d=1?

evidence.quote: We start with the simplest case: Periodic functions on [0,1], hence d = 1. Then a very simple algorithm has many optimality properties: Pick n \u2208 {m,m + 1,m + 2,...,2m} randomly and then take a randomly shifted midpoint rule with n function values and equal weights.

As an alternative, one can take n = 2m and first define, via interpolation at the Chebyshev points, a polynomial fm of degree smaller than m. Then we use separation of the main part together with the simplest Monte Carlo method for (f - fm) to obtain an almost optimal algorithm for each class Fk1.
Open Problem: Study and compare these algorithms (for d = 1) in more detail.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider one-dimensional numerical integration of a function f on the interval [0,1], i.e. approximation of the integral I(f) = ∫_0^1 f(x) dx. Two universal randomized quadrature strategies are defined as follows.

(A) Randomly shifted midpoint rule for periodic functions. Fix an integer m ≥ 1. Choose an integer n uniformly at random in {m, m+1, m+2, …, 2m}, and independently choose a shift τ uniformly at random in [0, 1/n]. Approximate I(f) by
   Q_A(f) = (1/n) ∑_{j=0}^{n-1} f( τ + (j + 1/2)/n  mod 1 ).
This algorithm is applied to 1-periodic functions f: ℝ → ℝ (extended periodically from [0,1]).

(B) Chebyshev interpolation plus Monte Carlo on the residual, for non-periodic functions. Fix m ≥ 1 and set n = 2m. Let f_m be the polynomial of degree less than m that interpolates f at the Chebyshev nodes x_i = (1 + cos((2i−1)π/(2m)))/2, i = 1,…,m. Compute I(f_m) exactly (separation of the main part). Then approximate I(f − f_m) by the simplest Monte Carlo estimator using m independent uniform samples ξ_1,…,ξ_m in [0,1]:
   Q_B(f) = I(f_m) + (1/m) ∑_{i=1}^m ( f(ξ_i) − f_m(ξ_i) ).

For standard function classes on [0,1] (e.g. Sobolev-type classes F_k^1 of functions with bounded k-th derivative, in both the periodic and non-periodic settings), give a detailed theoretical and practical comparison of the randomized algorithms Q_A and Q_B in dimension d = 1. In particular, determine and compare:
 (i) their root-mean-square errors sup_{f ∈ F} ( E |I(f) − Q(f)|^2 )^{1/2} as functions of m, including sharp constants where possible;
 (ii) the orders of optimal convergence achieved on each class, and whether either algorithm is universally (asymptotically) optimal across the scale of smoothness parameters k;
 (iii) their behavior on non-periodic vs. periodic functions, and the practical computational cost (number of function evaluations, arithmetic operations, numerical stability).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed explicitly as an open problem in a recent survey on optimal algorithms for numerical integration; no follow-up work appears to provide a detailed comparison of these two specific universal randomized one-dimensional algorithms. Each algorithm individually has known near-optimal error bounds, but a detailed theoretical and practical comparison appears not to have been carried out.
